title: I will have the opportunity to finally watch a movie at the institution I am studying at. What would you choose out of these films?

commenti.body:
Aguirre, The Wrath of God is easily my favorite from that list. A glorious sensory experience imbued with the poetry of Herzog's work. A masterpiece I keep returning to.

>Cleo from 5 to 7 sounds extremely interesting, yet is it mesmerizing in terms of philosophy, ideas and mood? Would you say it is a sad movie?  


Cleo I found to be mostly forgettable. I didn't find any interesting ideas in it, nor did it affect me emotionally much, although there are scenes that someone could find to be very sad. Maybe a bit harsh, but I personally find Varda to be massively overrated and one of the least engaging directors of the FNW. Just my opinion, no disrespect to anyone who loves her work.

Also huge fan of Network and Veronique, both being some of the best films ever made.

you should watch as many of these as you can. 

Here's my ranking...

* Network
* Aguirre, The Wrath of God 
* The Third Man
* The Long Goodbye
* The Double Life of Veronique
* Vivre Sa Vie
* Cleo from 5 to 7

Haven't seen these

* Incindies
* Le Mepris

But if you want to focus on the French films then that's good too. I'm obviously favoring the English language films.

Psycho - I'd rank this higher but it's not an art film and you'll have plenty of opportunity in life to see it. In fact, I would wait to watch it until after I've seen several Hitchcock films. Start with Strangers on a Train and work your way chronologically. You'll probably enjoy the films more that way.
I'd maybe recommend The Last Temptation of Christ by Scorsese or The Crucible by Hytner. Just watched these recently and they gave me that quality movie experience I was looking for.

That is very interesting to hear about, also, one of my great inspirations and forever admirations is David Lynch. What is your opinion on his body of work in all art?


Also, what is your opinion on Persona and Tarkovsky?


Thank you kindly.

I love several of these films.  Sidney Lumet’s “Network” is a chef d’œuvre, a masterpiece, on account of its über-eloquent script by the great Paddy Chayefsky; its performances; the sheer originality of the story.   

“Psycho” is another masterpiece, in my opinion, because of its largely unsung affinity to silent cinema, and to another masterfully literary script, this one by Joseph Stefano.  My favorite line:  “headaches are like resolutions: you forget them as soon as they stop hurting.”   I find “Psycho” to be a somber, rather nihilistic film, actually, that clashes jarringly with the Hollywood sensibility of that time period.   It really upset people in a way that Hitchcock films such as “Vertigo” or “Rear Window” did not.    In the novel “The Unbearable Lightness of Being,” one of the protagonist’s lovers tells him:  “You are the antithesis of kitsch.  In the world of kitsch, you would be a monster.”   That, to me, is Hitchcock’s “Psycho.”  The main taboo that it dares portray, in my estimation — alongside several others, which made the film rather scandalous, in its time— is the taboo of unhappiness.   Walt Disney was so disturbed by “Psycho” that he later refused to let “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” film on Disney property.   One of the most ingenious things about “Psycho” — in addition to its very dark, and  jarringly minimalist score by Bernard Hermann — is the performance of Anthony Perkins as Norman Bates.   Perkins called Norman the Hamlet of horror, and he brought his own brooding psychological complexity to the role.

“Contempt” by Godard — another great film, known in France for showcasing what Godard did with a big studio budget.  There’s a sadness in the film that is brought out by Georges Delarue’s elegiac score, which Scorsese would see fit to use to bring out the sadness in his own film “Casino.”   Godard’s “Contempt” is also a feast, linguistically:  French, English, German, Italian are all spoken onscreen.

“The Third Man” — the cinematography; the theme of nihilism….  I’ve commented too much above not to refrain from bringing my comments to a close, but it’s a film that I find intensely philosophical in the vein of “what if nothing is true, and everything is permitted?”   The visuals draw upon German expressionist cinema — disorienting “Dutch angles,” as they’re called,  which is really referring to German Expressionist  (Deutsch) camera angles — and the theme of the film portrays the disorientation of a post-World War II world in which any notion of a reassuring moral compass is absent.   A hundred years earlier, a thinker such as Emerson had written:  “Oh my brothers, God exists.  There is a soul at the center of nature and and over the will of every man so that none of us can wrong the universe.  It has so infused its strong enchantment into nature, that we prosper when we accept its advice and when we struggle to wound its creatures, our hands are glued to our sides, or they beat our own breasts.”  In comparison, the sensibility of “The Third Man” is jaded and world-weary; all comfortable moral certainties gone.  It exists very much in the zeitgeist of the immediate post-war era, in the aftermath of something like close to a tenth of a billion victims (in World War II), and where civilian deaths outnumbered military ones by a ratio of around three to one.
Way wrong about Varda. Maybe you don't like Cleo and that's fine but besides Godard she is the most ambitious and innovative and has the most to say among the FNW. You need to re-assess her work.

> and has the most to say among the FNW.

In what sense? I'm curious. I find both Rohmer and Rivette in particular to be light-years ahead of her.

>What is your opinion on his body of work in all art?

He's easily one of my top filmmakers. I love every feature film he has made, even Dune to a certain extent as silly as that film is, and Twin Peaks is my favorite TV show.  Can't say I ever got much from his paintings or albums though, but they're okay.

>Also, what is your opinion on Persona and Tarkovsky?

Persona's not for me. Always disliked how Bergman wrote women, and Persona is one of the worst examples of that. The story about the beach orgy in the film was especially bad with how blatantly it had been written by a horny dude. I'll have to thank a few female friends of mine for telling me how clueless Bergman was about women.

Tarkovsky is fine. A master on a technical level, for sure. His most religious works are too culturally alien for me, as I don't find his Orthodox Christian worldview very appealing or interesting.

Firstly, thank you kindly for this warm message, sometimes when people spend time trying to communicate this eloquently with another human being, it fills me with a reverence towards our beautiful civilization.


There is an element of generosity to be found in such beautiful interactions which makes me gain hope in all things.


I watch films because I believe they contain sincerity of people in them, more so, the ability to transcend the ego and all the little problems we invent for ourselves to give us the illusion of importance and allows us to swim in the grand constellation of universal love.


Speaking of that, also, what do you personally think of Tarkovsky? Or Bergman? Persona seems quite profound and also really superb.


Also, there are some movies I really want to watch like They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?, The Umbrellas of Cherbourg and Vivre sa Vie, do you like these movies?


Would you say Psycho is about the misery, the pain, the emptiness, fatigue and lethargy of being, of existing with people and of just not feeling good with oneself?


Also, may I ask you about the idea of watching a film. In the past I kept googling the message or meaning of it because I always felt like I would enjoy it more if I had known its message, its theme or its meaning so I can fully love the experience.


Do you think going in without external definitions of the movie and just letting its pure experience absorb you is a better way?


Thank you kindly.

Those just happen to be a couple of the directors I am least familiar with 😂

I've never seen a Rivette film, but I've seen a couple Rohmer films, which I really enjoyed, but I think in comparison he seems very focused on the domestic/romantic life of the middle class, from what little I know of him.

Varda on the other hand consistently covers a wide range of subjects, with all sorts of different kinds of people. Vagabond is a good example of a story that tackles quite a lot, big questions about society, homelessness, capitalism, socialism, dignity and compassion/forgiveness, death and the value of a single life, a woman who is considered "worthless," but who affected both the very wealthy and the very poor, and many in between. One of my favorite movies.

Stylistically she is very audacious, beats to the sound of her own drum. La Pointe Courte, which mixes fiction and documentary, about a rural fishing village, is very dreamy in a way that reminds me of Herzog and Bergman.

The obvious contribution that's lacking in the other FNW films is she offers a woman's perspective, which is something that really stands out in Cleo as well as Le Bonheur.

And she doesn't limit herself to fiction, she has wonderful documentaries, most famously The Gleaners and I.

Anyway, I love her. Hope I didn't come off too aggressive with my previous comment, I just don't believe she should be dismissed.

Pauline Kael loved it, that beach scene. 

That scene scared me, when I first saw it, because it portrayed a sexual desire — a female sexual desire, in this case —  that was uncontrollable. “Off the rails.”

Now that I’ve reached my late 40’s, I know from experience that such female sexual desire exists.   I think that women, themselves, can be surprised and blind-sighted by it, when it emerges with such unbridled force.  

I think a film like “Eyes Wide Shut,” which I’m not keen about for a few different reasons, nonetheless gets right that the different facets of women’s sexual desire are not well understood.   “Millions of years of commitment…  Men have to stick it in whoever they can, but for women it’s about security, and commitment… If you men only knew.”   

I’m not a fan of Kael (mostly, I admit, because of the way in which she analyzed Kubrick).  But here, I think, I agree with her in the implication that female sexuality is not being travestied by a male sensibility.  And , it would seem, Kubrick in EWS agreed.

“There is a brief passage in Ingmar Bergman‘s Persona — Bibi Andersson tells about a day and night of sex — that is so much more erotic than all of Ulysses that it demonstrates what can be done on the screen with told material. We do not need to see images of the beach and the boy and the return to the fiancee that she describes because the excitement is in how she tells it. Bergman has the capacity to create images that set off reverberations: in the early part of Illicit Interlude an old woman appears for just a moment on a road — walking — and this image, like the croquet game in Smiles of a Summer Night, seems to be suspended in time. In moments like these, Bergman is a great artist. In Persona Bibi Andersson’s almost fierce revery has that kind of beauty. As she goes on talking, with memories of summer and nakedness and pleasure in her words and the emptiness of her present in her face, we begin to hold our breath in fear that Bergman can’t sustain this almost intolerably difficult sequence. But he does, and it builds and builds and is completed. It’s one of the rare, truly erotic sequences on film.”

Thank you, too, very much.  I’m smiling, having read your message to me. 

“Persona” is my favorite Bergman film and a masterpiece, in my opinion.   I actually had regretted, in reading your original description of film choices, that “Persona” was not among them.  

My reading of “Persona” is, again, quite nihilistic.   The existentialists wrote about “authenticity” — sincerity, genuineness — and the 20th century Jung wrote of the Persona, the social mask that we wear, as a result of acculturation and the weight of social expectations, as opposed to the Self.

What Bergman is at least contemplating in “Persona,” as I see it, is the possibility that this real, substantial Self does not exist, just as a soul (created by God) does not exist.  Instead, all is Persona, layers upon layers of appearance.  Elisabeth Vogler is trying to be authentic, to renounce the mask and to live an authentic, true self.   Bergman is considering, as I see it, that this is yet another performance, another donning of a mask, and that she is *playing * at being authentic.  And why? Because the spiritual core of the human being may not, in fact, exist.   

Then there’s the fact that the self, identity, is so fragile a thing, so much of an epiphenomenon (a superficial byproduct of elements it imbibes, including from its environment) that the two women in such intimate contact with each other *can* being to merge because the walls of identity are permeable, unstable, to begin with.   It’s like peeling an onion and, once one has peeled, one is left with nothing.   

The Buddhists could agree with all this — no Self; no independent identity — yet Bergman’s orientation is more pessimistic.

Bergman, to me, is a skeptic.  Tarkovsky is a spiritualist.  Tarkovsky’s films can seem overwhelming to me because the work of other filmmakers can seem rather pedestrian, in comparison.   Not nearly as high-minded, or elevated in sensibility.   This is the only filmmaker I’ve encountered that not only has a hypnotic quality to his work, but that can *induce* in viewers something akin to a state of hypnosis.  Time can seem to slow down.  One can be lifted up to a heightened state of awareness, as if in a trance state or reverie.  I experienced that, I felt, in watching “Nostalghia” in the theater and never forgot it.  My heart rate, my breathing, were altered, even after I walked out of the theater.  I was inhabiting a state of hyper awareness that lasted for at least the next thirty minutes or so.  The quality of my perception just felt different.   No other filmmaker I’ve ever experienced could do that for me.  

Which is not to say that I’ve not struggled with Tarkovsky… Nor that I count him as a favorite.  But I did have this experience, watching “Nostalghia” on the big screen — and felt something like it, albeit not as sustained, watching other of his films — and so have to give credit where credit is due.  

I don’t have strong feelings against forgoing analysis and just experiencing the film.   For me, somehow, I no longer experience it as a dichotomy or either/or proposition:  analyze the film, *or* enjoy it more viscerally.  I do like any *understanding* I have of a film to be organic, unforced.  That is, I don’t like interpretations that are a stretch.  In a film like “Persona,” the questioning of “What if there *is* no real self and it’s all just personae, masks upon masks, behind which there is no solid identity?” is something I feel is emanating from the film, as opposed to something I’m cleverly trying to impose upon it.   

I think it’s true that *theme * does exist in works of art — ideas that the artist is exploring, questions they are asking within the work itself.  To give an example, in “The Godfather,” there is the tragic theme of a protagonist who is as constrained, as controlled by outside circumstances,  as a puppet on a string;  that image of the strings is both Vito’s hope for his son (that he will be the ones *holding them *, one day) and his own fate.  For one thing, no one else in the family was capable of stepping up to fill his father’s shoes.   It had to be him.   For another, he loved his father, and perceived that his father’s life was being threatened, and that only he, within the family, had the wherewithal to do something about it.  Would expecting him to have had the real *freedom* to act differently than he did be tantamount to expecting someone to have the freedom to be cut, yet not to bleed?
